mainTopic: Hidden righteous people (אבא אומנא, רבא, רבי ברוקא's market), then the משנה's disasters that call for sounding the alarm: blight, locusts, rampaging beasts, and the sword
overview: This amud finishes the story of אבא אומנא, the bloodletter whom Heaven greeted every day. The חכמים test him by taking his rugs. He names a plain price, assumes they needed the money for פדיון שבויים, and had already given the rugs to צדקה. רבא is then comforted for receiving heavenly greetings less often than אביי: his merit protects his whole city. Next, אליהו הנביא shows רבי ברוקא חוזאה hidden people with a share in עולם הבא. One is a disguised Jewish jailer who protects women and warns the חכמים about decrees. Two others are brothers who cheer up sad people and make peace. The גמרא then returns to the משנה's list of disasters for which the alarm is sounded everywhere. It explains when a wild animal counts as מְשׁוּלַּחַת, using tests of place, time, and behavior, and settles several contradictions in the ברייתא. Finally, it teaches that even a passing 'sword of peace' calls for an alarm, proven from פרעה נכה and המלך יאשיהו, with the verse coming on the next amud.

steps.title: The חכמים take the rugs to market and test אבא אומנא's honesty
steps.stepSummary: In the morning the חכמים roll up אבא אומנא's rugs and take them to the market. They ask him to name the rugs' value. He gives an honest price, and then they reveal the rugs are his.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the morning they rolled up the rugs, took them, and went out to the market, and there they met him. They said to him: 'Let the master tell us what these are worth.' He said: 'Such and such.' They said: 'Maybe they are worth more?' He said: 'This is what I paid for them.' They said: 'They are yours, and we took them from you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים who slept at אבא אומנא's house took his rugs and now test whether he will be honest about their value. Then they admit the rugs are his.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the חכמים push him with 'maybe they are worth more?', he answers 'this is what I paid for them.' That shows he recognized the rugs as his own, yet he still gave a plain price and accused no one. The חכמים then admit the rugs are his, which sets up the next question: why did he say nothing?

keyTerms.meaning: Let him appraise; estimate the value

steps.confusionAlert: This is the continuation of a story that began earlier. The 'they' are two חכמים sent by אביי to test אבא אומנא, who had hosted them overnight and given them these rugs to sleep on. They were not stealing. They were testing his character.

phrases.english: In the morning, they rolled them up and took them
phrases.notes: 'Them' refers to the rugs that אבא אומנא gave his guests.

phrases.english: and they got up and went out to the market, and he found them (they met him there).

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: לְשַׁיְּימֵיהּ מָר הֵיכִי שָׁווּ.
phrases.english: They said to him: Let the master appraise how much they are worth.
He said to them: Such and such.
They said to him: But perhaps they are worth more?
He said to them: This is what I paid for them.
phrases.notes: The parentheses and brackets show a textual correction. The corrected reading is שקלי להו, 'I bought them.'

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: דִּידָךְ נִיהוּ וְשַׁקְלִינְהוּ מִינָּךְ.
phrases.english: They said to him: They are yours, and we took them from you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the אבא אומנא testing story from the previous part of the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אבא אומנא was honest even when pricing his own stolen goods, and he never accused anyone.

steps.title: The חכמים ask what אבא אומנא suspected them of
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים ask אבא אומנא what he thought when he noticed they had taken his rugs.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: 'Please tell us, what did you suspect us of?'
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים ask a sincere question: you knew we took your rugs, so what did you think of us? This sets up אבא's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Any normal person would assume theft. The question pushes אבא to reveal his inner attitude toward the people who seemed to wrong him.

phrases.english: They said to him: Please, we beg of you,
what did you suspect us of?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows the reveal that the חכמים took his rugs.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What אבא אומנא thought about the people who took his property.

steps.title: אבא אומנא judged them favorably: פדיון שבויים
steps.stepSummary: אבא אומנא answers that he assumed the חכמים needed money urgently for פדיון שבויים and were too embarrassed to ask him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: 'I told myself that an opportunity to redeem captives had come up for the rabbis, and they were embarrassed to ask me.'
steps.whatsHappening: אבא explains that he never suspected them of theft. He assumed they had a holy, urgent need.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the high point of דן לכף זכות, judging others favorably. He did not merely excuse them. He imagined the most noble reason possible, a מצוה of פדיון שבויים, and even protected their dignity by assuming they were too embarrassed to ask.

keyTerms.meaning: Redeeming captives, a very great מצוה

steps.whyThisMatters: This answer is a classic model of judging others favorably, and it helps explain why אבא אומנא merited daily greetings from Heaven.

phrases.english: He said to them: I said (to myself),
a ransom of captives came up for the rabbis,
and they were embarrassed to tell me.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He assumed they took the rugs for פדיון שבויים and were too ashamed to ask.

steps.title: אבא אומנא refuses to take the rugs back: already given to צדקה
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים offer to return the rugs. אבא refuses, because from the moment he noticed them missing he had mentally given them to צדקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: 'Now let the master take them back!' He said: 'From that moment, I removed them from my mind for צדקה.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story of אבא אומנא ends. Even when he could have his property back, he would not take what he had already dedicated to צדקה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His generosity was not only in his thoughts. Once he decided the rugs were for צדקה, he treated that decision as final. This completes the picture of his greatness: honest, judging favorably, and generous.

keyTerms.meaning: I removed them from my mind; I gave up ownership in my thoughts

steps.whatToRemember: אבא אומנא passed every test: he priced the rugs honestly, judged the חכמים favorably by assuming פדיון שבויים, and stood by his mental dedication of the rugs to צדקה.

phrases.english: They said to him: Now, let the master take them!
He said to them: From that moment,
I put them out of my mind for charity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Final exchange of the אבא אומנא story.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: אבא אומנא's righteousness was complete, which is why Heaven greeted him daily.

steps.title: רבא is comforted: his merit protects his whole city
steps.stepSummary: רבא felt bad that אביי received heavenly greetings more often than he did. Heaven told him that he protects his entire city.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא was upset because of אביי. They said to him: 'Be satisfied that you protect the whole city.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the background of the story. אביי got greetings every ערב שבת, רבא only every ערב יום כיפור, and רבא is now comforted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The comparison was about how often each one received a heavenly greeting. Heaven answers that רבא has a different kind of greatness: his merit shields the whole city. Not getting greetings as often does not mean having less worth.

keyTerms.meaning: It is enough for you; be satisfied

steps.confusionAlert: 'They said to him' here means Heaven, not people. Also, 'because of אביי' refers to אביי getting greetings more often (every ערב שבת). It does not mean אביי did something wrong to רבא.

phrases.english: Rava was distressed
because of Abaye (who received greetings more often),
They (from Heaven) said to him: Be content
that you protect the entire city.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲוָה קָא חָלְשָׁא דַּעְתֵּיהּ דְּרָבָא מִשּׁוּם דְּאַבָּיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the larger frame story of heavenly greetings to אבא אומנא, אביי, and רבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבא's greatness is that his merit protects his whole city.

steps.title: רבי ברוקא asks אליהו if anyone in the market merits עולם הבא
steps.stepSummary: A new story begins. רבי ברוקא חוזאה, who often met אליהו הנביא in the market of בי לפט, asks whether anyone there has a share in עולם הבא. אליהו says no.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ברוקא חוזאה was often in the market of בי לפט, and אליהו often appeared to him. He asked: 'Is there anyone in this market who is a בן עולם הבא?' אליהו said: 'No.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new story about hidden righteous people. This step sets up the scene and the question, and the surprising answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The setting is an ordinary, busy market. אליהו's first answer, 'no one,' makes what follows stand out even more, because he will soon point to someone after all.

keyTerms.meaning: One who has a share in עולם הבא

phrases.english: Rabbi Beroka of Ḥoza
was often found in the market of Bei Lefet.
Elijah would often appear to him.
He said to him: Is there in this market
anyone worthy of the World to Come?
He said to him: No.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי בְּרוֹקָא חוֹזָאָה הֲוָה שְׁכִיחַ בְּשׁוּקָא דְּבֵי לָפָט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story on the same theme: the hidden greatness of ordinary people.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether anyone in the market merits עולם הבא.

steps.title: אליהו points to an unlikely man dressed like a non-Jew
steps.stepSummary: רבי ברוקא sees a man wearing black shoes and no ציצית with תכלת. אליהו says this man is a בן עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Meanwhile he saw a man wearing black shoes, who did not put the blue thread of ציצית on his cloak. אליהו said: 'This one is a בן עולם הבא.'
steps.whatsHappening: אליהו surprisingly points to the person who looks the least religious. The גמרא is setting up an explanation of why this man is so great, which steps 8-13 give.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Black shoes were not the Jewish custom, and he wore no ציצית. By appearance he looked like he did not care about מצוות. Yet אליהו singles him out, which teaches that outward appearance can hide great righteousness.

keyTerms.meaning: Meanwhile; in the middle of this

steps.confusionAlert: Do not conclude that wearing black shoes or skipping ציצית is praiseworthy. The גמרא will soon explain that this man had a special reason for dressing this way, connected to the important work he was doing.

phrases.english: In the meantime, he saw a certain man
who was wearing black shoes
and did not put the sky-blue thread on his cloak.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הַאי בַּר עָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי הוּא.
phrases.english: He (Elijah) said to him: This one is worthy of the World to Come.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Surprisingly revises אליהו's 'no' by identifying one person in the market who merits עולם הבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A man who looks non-observant is identified as a בן עולם הבא.

steps.title: רבי ברוקא chases the man and asks what he does
steps.stepSummary: רבי ברוקא runs after the man and asks about his occupation. The man tells him to go away and come back tomorrow.
steps.simpleTranslation: He ran after him and said: What is your work? The man said: Go now, and come back tomorrow.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ברוקא wants to know what this strange-looking man does that earns him עולם הבא, so he chases him and asks. The man puts him off until tomorrow, which sets up the rest of the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From the last step, this man looked like the opposite of a צדיק: black shoes and no ציצית. So רבי ברוקא's question is really: what hidden deeds make up for this outside appearance? The man's odd answer ("come back tomorrow") is a small puzzle that the גמרא will explain later.

keyTerms.meaning: What is your work / what do you do?

phrases.english: He (Rabbi Beroka) ran after him
He said to him: What is your occupation?
He said to him: Go away now,
and come back tomorrow.
phrases.notes: The reason for this delay is explained in step 13.

steps.triggerLanguage: רְהַט בָּתְרֵיהּ, אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי עוֹבָדָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on אליהו's surprising statement that this man is a בן עולם הבא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does this man do that earns him עולם הבא?

steps.title: The man is a jailer who protects modesty and saves Jewish women
steps.stepSummary: The next day the man explains that he is a prison guard. He keeps men and women apart to prevent sin, and he risks his life to save Jewish women from non-Jews, once by making a girl look like a נדה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The next day he asked again: What is your work? He said: I am a jailer. I lock up the men separately and the women separately, and I put my bed between them so they won't sin. When I see a Jewish girl that non-Jews have their eyes on, I risk my life to save her. One day there was an engaged girl with us that non-Jews had their eyes on. I took red wine dregs, threw them on the bottom of her dress, and said: She is a נדה.
steps.whatsHappening: The man answers רבי ברוקא's question: he is a Jewish jailer who quietly guards the moral purity of the prisoners.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His job looks ordinary, but he uses it to prevent sin, even sleeping between the men and the women himself. He also risks his life to protect Jewish women. The wine trick worked because the non-Jews would stay away from a woman they thought was menstruating.

phrases.english: The next day he said to him: What is your occupation?
He said to him: I am a prison guard,
and I lock up the men separately and the women separately,
and I place my bed between these and those

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלָא לֵיתוֹ לִידֵי אִיסּוּרָא.
phrases.english: so that they will not come to sin.
When I see a Jewish woman
that non-Jews have set their eyes upon,
I risk my life and save her.

phrases.aramaic: יוֹמָא חַד הֲווֹת נַעֲרָה מְאוֹרָסָה גַּבַּן
phrases.english: One day there was a betrothed young woman among us
that non-Jews had set their eyes on,
I took dregs of red wine
and threw them on the lower part of her dress,
and I said: She is menstruating.
phrases.notes: So the non-Jews would leave her alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 8, one day later.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He is a jailer who prevents sin among the prisoners and risks his life to protect Jewish women.

steps.title: Why no ציצית and why black shoes?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ברוקא asks why the man has no ציצית threads and wears black shoes.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Why don't you have ציצית threads, and why do you wear black shoes?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ברוקא now asks about the man's strange way of dressing, which made him look like he was not a religious Jew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man's good deeds were explained, but his outer appearance still seems to clash with being a בן עולם הבא. This question goes after that leftover puzzle.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי טַעְמָא לֵית לָךְ חוּטֵי,
phrases.english: He said to him: Why do you not have (ציצית) threads,
and why do you wear black shoes?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After hearing his deeds, רבי ברוקא asks about the man's non-Jewish-looking clothing.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why does he dress in a way that hides his Jewishness?

steps.title: He hides his Jewishness to warn the חכמים about decrees
steps.stepSummary: The man explains that he moves among non-Jews and must not be recognized as a Jew. That way he learns about harsh decrees and tells the חכמים, who pray and get the decrees cancelled.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: I come and go among non-Jews, so I dress this way so they won't know I am a Jew. When they make a decree, I tell the חכמים, and they pray and the decree is cancelled.
steps.whatsHappening: The man explains that his clothing is a disguise. It lets him hear about dangerous decrees so he can warn the Jewish community.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His outer look is not a lack of care for מצוות. It is a cover that lets him protect the whole Jewish community. Because he looks like a non-Jew, he hears secret plans and passes them to the חכמים, whose prayers cancel the decrees.

keyTerms.meaning: I go in and out (I move among them)

steps.confusionAlert: The story is not praising skipping ציצית or wearing black shoes in themselves. It is praising someone whose disguise served a life-saving purpose for the community.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: עָיֵילְנָא וְנָפֵיקְנָא בֵּינֵי נׇכְרִים,
phrases.english: He said to him: I come and go among non-Jews,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלָא לִידְּעוּ דִּיהוּדָאָה אֲנָא.
phrases.english: (I dress this way) so that they will not know that I am a Jew.
When they make a decree,
I inform the Sages,
and they pray for mercy and cancel their decree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the clothing question from step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: His disguise lets him learn of decrees and warn the חכמים so they can pray.

steps.title: Why did you tell me to come back tomorrow?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ברוקא asks why the man put him off the day before.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why, when I asked you what your work was, did you tell me: Go now and come back tomorrow?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ברוקא goes back to the puzzle from step 8: why did the man send him away the first time?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ties up the loose end left open in step 8. The answer will show that even the delay was part of his work for the community.

phrases.aramaic: וּמַאי טַעְמָא כִּי אָמֵינָא לָךְ אֲנָא מַאי עוֹבָדָךְ,
phrases.english: And why, when I said to you: What is your occupation,

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲמַרְתְּ לִי: זִיל הָאִידָּנָא וְתָא לִמְחַר?
phrases.english: did you say to me: Go away now and come back tomorrow?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאי טַעְמָא כִּי אָמֵינָא לָךְ אֲנָא מַאי עוֹבָדָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the unexplained delay from step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason for the man's delay the day before.

steps.title: A decree had just been made, so he rushed to warn the חכמים
steps.stepSummary: The man explains that a decree had just been issued at that moment. He had to hurry and tell the חכמים so they could pray.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: At that very moment they made a decree. I said to myself: First I will go and hear it, and send word to the חכמים so they will pray about this matter.
steps.whatsHappening: The man explains that he was in the middle of an emergency: a new decree had just been made, and warning the חכמים came first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saving the community could not wait, even for a conversation with a great sage. This finishes the portrait of this hidden צדיק: everything about him, even his rudeness, came from his work for others.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: בְּהַהִיא שַׁעְתָּא גָּזְרִי גְּזֵירְתָּא,
phrases.english: He said to him: At that moment they had made a decree,
and I said: First I will go and hear (and report) it,
and send word to the Sages
so that they will pray for mercy about the matter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the delay and closes the jailer episode.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A decree had just been issued, and alerting the חכמים came first.

steps.title: אליהו points out two brothers who also have a share in עולם הבא
steps.stepSummary: Two brothers arrive, and אליהו הנביא tells רבי ברוקא that they are also בני עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Meanwhile, two brothers came. אליהו said to him: These two also have a share in עולם הבא.
steps.whatsHappening: A second surprising example begins. אליהו points to two more people, and this sets up the next question about what they do.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the jailer, these brothers do not look like obvious צדיקים. The story repeats its pattern: אליהו makes a surprising statement, and then רבי ברוקא finds out the hidden reason.

phrases.aramaic: אַדְּהָכִי וְהָכִי אֲתוֹ הָנָךְ תְּרֵי אַחֵי.
phrases.english: Meanwhile, these two brothers came.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָנָךְ נָמֵי בְּנֵי עָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי נִינְהוּ.
phrases.english: (אליהו) said to him: These too are people of the World to Come.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַדְּהָכִי וְהָכִי אֲתוֹ הָנָךְ תְּרֵי אַחֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second example in the same pattern as step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: These two brothers have a share in עולם הבא.

steps.title: רבי ברוקא asks the brothers what they do
steps.stepSummary: רבי ברוקא goes over to the brothers and asks about their occupation.
steps.simpleTranslation: He went to them and said: What is your work?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ברוקא asks the same question he asked the jailer. This sets up the brothers' answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The repeated question "מאי עובדך" shows that the story is looking for the deed behind the reward each time.

phrases.english: He went over to them,
and said to them: What is your occupation?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲזַל לְגַבַּיְיהוּ, אֲמַר לְהוּ: מַאי עוֹבָדַיְיכוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on אליהו's statement about the brothers.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What deeds earn the brothers עולם הבא?

steps.title: The brothers cheer up sad people and make peace
steps.stepSummary: The brothers explain that they are jesters who cheer up sad people, and they work to make peace between people who are fighting.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: We are cheerful people who cheer up the sad. Also, when we see two people who have a fight between them, we work hard to make peace between them.
steps.whatsHappening: The brothers answer: their "job" is making people happy and bringing peace.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Simple kindness, like lifting someone's mood or ending a quarrel, is enough to earn עולם הבא. Together with the jailer, the story teaches that great merit can be hidden in ordinary-looking people.
steps.whatToRemember: The story of רבי ברוקא teaches that עולם הבא can belong to people who look plain or even irreligious on the outside: a jailer who protects others and quietly saves the community, and jesters who cheer up sad people and make peace.

phrases.english: They said to him: We are jesters,
we cheer up the sad.

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי, כִּי חָזֵינַן בֵּי תְרֵי
phrases.english: Also, when we see two people
who have a quarrel between them,
we make an effort and make peace between them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 15 and closes the story of רבי ברוקא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They cheer up the sad and make peace between people who are fighting.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: disasters for which the alarm is sounded everywhere
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה and brings a ברייתא listing the disasters for which the alarm is sounded in every place: blight, mildew, locusts, caterpillars, and wild beasts.
steps.simpleTranslation: "For these they sound the alarm in every place", etc. The Rabbis taught: For these they sound the alarm in every place: for blight, for mildew, for locusts and caterpillars, and for dangerous beasts.
steps.whatsHappening: The story section is over, and the גמרא returns to the next line of the משנה. It brings a ברייתא that lists which disasters call for an alarm everywhere.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Most disasters only require an alarm in the place where they happen. These disasters spread from place to place, so even people in other places sound the alarm. The ברייתא gives the basic list, and רבי עקיבא will add details in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: They sound the alarm (with fasting, prayer, and shofar)

steps.confusionAlert: "בכל מקום" does not mean the disaster is happening everywhere. It means that even places not yet hit sound the alarm, because these disasters spread.

phrases.aramaic: עַל אֵלּוּ מַתְרִיעִין בְּכׇל מָקוֹם כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: (The Mishnah:) For these they sound the alarm in every place, etc.

phrases.aramaic: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן, עַל אֵלּוּ מַתְרִיעִין בְּכׇל מָקוֹם:
phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: For these they sound the alarm in every place:
for blight, and for mildew,

phrases.aramaic: וְעַל אַרְבֶּה וְחָסִיל, וְעַל חַיָּה רָעָה.
phrases.english: and for locusts and caterpillars, and for dangerous beasts.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the aggadah and returns to the משנה's halachic list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The alarm is sounded everywhere for blight, mildew, locusts, caterpillars, and dangerous beasts.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: even a small amount triggers the alarm
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא says that for blight and mildew, any amount is enough to sound the alarm. For locusts, even one wing seen anywhere in ארץ ישראל is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא says: For blight and mildew, any amount. For locusts and caterpillars, even if only one wing was seen in ארץ ישראל, they sound the alarm for them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא adds a rule about how much of the disaster has to be present before the alarm is sounded.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion gave the list but did not say how much damage is needed. רבי עקיבא sets the bar very low: even a tiny sign is enough. One wing is a warning that a swarm is on the way.
steps.whatToRemember: These spreading disasters call for an alarm in every place. According to רבי עקיבא, even the smallest sign, like any blight or a single locust wing, is enough.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: עַל הַשִּׁדָּפוֹן וְעַל הַיֵּרָקוֹן בְּכׇל שֶׁהוּא.
phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says: For blight and for mildew, (they sound the alarm) over any amount.
Locusts and caterpillars,

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ לֹא נִרְאָה בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶלָּא כָּנָף אֶחָד —
phrases.english: even if only a single wing was seen in the Land of Israel
they sound the alarm over them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a minimum-amount rule to the ברייתא's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Any amount of blight or mildew, or even a single locust wing seen in ארץ ישראל, is enough to sound the alarm.

steps.title: A dangerous animal triggers the alarm only when it is on a rampage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's words about a dangerous beast and brings a ברייתא: the alarm is sounded only if the animal is מְשׁוּלַּחַת.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said the alarm is sounded for a beast. The Rabbis taught: the 'dangerous beast' they mentioned means one that is on a rampage. Then they sound the alarm. If it is not on a rampage, they do not sound the alarm.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the last item in the משנה's list, the dangerous animal, and brings a ברייתא that limits when it counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wild animals exist all the time, so not every animal sighting is a disaster. The ברייתא says the alarm is only for an animal that is מְשׁוּלַּחַת, acting out of its normal nature, which suggests a punishment from Heaven. This sets up the next question: how do we know when an animal counts as מְשׁוּלַּחַת?

keyTerms.meaning: 'Sent loose' or on a rampage, acting abnormally
They sound the alarm (with fasting and prayer)

steps.confusionAlert: Here מְשׁוּלַּחַת does not just mean an animal wandering loose. It describes an animal acting out of character and invading people's space, which shows it is a sign of punishment.

phrases.english: 'And for a beast, etc.'
The Rabbis taught:
The 'dangerous beast' that they mentioned
when it is on a rampage, they sound the alarm over it;
if it is not on a rampage, they do not sound the alarm over it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues down the משנה's list of disasters from step 17, now explaining the last one, the dangerous beast.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The alarm is sounded for a dangerous animal only when it is מְשׁוּלַּחַת.

steps.title: Signs of a rampage by place and by time
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא defines מְשׁוּלַּחַת: seen in the city it counts, in the field it does not; seen by day it counts, at night it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which animal is on a rampage, and which is not? If it is seen in the city, it is on a rampage. If it is seen in the field, it is not. If it is seen by day, it is on a rampage. If it is seen at night, it is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks its own question, what counts as מְשׁוּלַּחַת, and answers with two tests: place and time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The logic is about normal versus abnormal behavior. Animals normally live in fields and come out at night, so seeing them there or then is not unusual. An animal in the city or out in daylight is acting against its nature.

keyTerms.meaning: Which one is it? (asks for a definition)

phrases.english: Which animal is considered on a rampage
and which is not on a rampage?
If it is seen in the city, it is on a rampage;
in the field, it is not on a rampage.
By day, it is on a rampage;
at night, it is not on a rampage.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵי זוֹ הִיא מְשׁוּלַּחַת וְאֵי זוֹ הִיא שֶׁאֵינָהּ מְשׁוּלַּחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the term מְשׁוּלַּחַת that was introduced in step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: City sighting counts, field sighting does not; day sighting counts, night sighting does not.

steps.title: Signs of a rampage by the animal's behavior
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds behavior tests: chasing people, killing more than it eats, or snatching a baby from a crib are signs of a rampage. Hiding, or eating everything it kills, are not.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it saw two people and chased them, it is on a rampage. If it hid from them, it is not. If it killed two people and ate only one, it is on a rampage. If it ate both, it is not. If it climbed onto a roof and took a baby from its crib, it is on a rampage.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues and gives signs based on how the animal acts toward people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A normal animal fears people or kills only from hunger. Chasing people, killing more than it needs, or invading a home shows it is acting against its nature. An animal that eats both people was simply hungry, so that is natural behavior.

keyTerms.meaning: It tore apart, killed as prey

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the main test behind all the rules: the alarm is for unnatural animal behavior, not for an animal acting as animals normally do.

phrases.english: If it saw two people
and ran after them, it is on a rampage.
If it hid from them, it is not on a rampage.
If it killed two people
and ate one of them, it is on a rampage.
If it ate both of them, it is not on a rampage.
phrases.notes: It was just hungry, which is natural.

phrases.english: If it climbed onto the roof
and took a baby from a cradle, it is on a rampage.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָאֲתָה שְׁנֵי בְּנֵי אָדָם וְרָצְתָה אַחֲרֵיהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds behavior-based signs after the place and time signs of step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Chasing people, killing more than it eats, or snatching a baby from a home counts as מְשׁוּלַּחַת; hiding or eating all it kills does not.

steps.title: The ברייתא seems to contradict itself about city and night
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out a problem: 'seen in the city counts' implies day or night, but 'at night it does not count' says otherwise.
steps.simpleTranslation: This ברייתא contradicts itself. You said: if it is seen in the city, it is on a rampage, which means it makes no difference whether by day or by night. Then you said: by day it is on a rampage, at night it is not!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא from inside itself, showing that two of its rules seem to clash.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first rule makes the city the only test, so a city sighting at night should count. The second rule makes time the test, so a night sighting should not count, even in the city. Both cannot be true for an animal seen in the city at night.

keyTerms.meaning: This source itself is difficult (it contradicts itself)

phrases.english: This ברייתא itself is difficult:
you said, if it is seen in the city, it is on a rampage,

phrases.aramaic: לָא שְׁנָא בַּיּוֹם וְלָא שְׁנָא בַּלַּיְלָה.
phrases.english: no matter whether by day or by night.
And then you said:
by day it is on a rampage, at night it is not!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the place and time rules of step 20 and finds a clash between them.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two tests in the ברייתא (city versus field, and day versus night).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Internal contradiction: the city rule implies a city sighting at night counts, while the time rule implies any night sighting does not count.

steps.title: Both conditions are needed: city and daytime
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the two rules work together. Only a city sighting by day counts. A city sighting at night, or a field sighting even by day, does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not a problem. This is what the ברייתא means: if it is seen in the city by day, it is on a rampage. In the city at night, it is not. Likewise, in the field, even by day, it is not. (In the field at night, it is not.)
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction by reading the ברייתא's two rules as one combined rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא was not giving two separate tests. It was giving two conditions that must both be met: the city and the daytime. If either one is missing, it is not a rampage, so there is no contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; the problem is answered
This is what it means (rereading the source)

steps.whatToRemember: An animal is מְשׁוּלַּחַת only if it is seen in the city by day. The behavior signs (chasing people, killing without eating, taking a baby) also show a rampage.
steps.confusionAlert: Usually אִי נָמֵי introduces a second, different answer. Here it does not. It just continues the list of cases inside the same answer.

phrases.english: It is not difficult; this is what it is saying:
if it is seen in the city by day, it is on a rampage;
in the city at night, it is not on a rampage.

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי בַּשָּׂדֶה, אֲפִילּוּ בַּיּוֹם — אֵינָהּ מְשׁוּלַּחַת.
phrases.english: Likewise, in the field, even by day, it is not on a rampage.
(In the field at night, it is not on a rampage.)
phrases.notes: This is obvious, since neither condition is met.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the source: the two rules are combined into one rule with two required conditions.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא gave two independent tests, so a city sighting at night would count under one and fail under the other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both conditions are required. Only a city sighting by day counts as מְשׁוּלַּחַת.

steps.title: Does a beast that just stands still count as rampaging?
steps.stepSummary: Two clauses of the ברייתא seem to give opposite rules for an animal that stands its ground.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא says that if the animal saw two people and chased them, it is on a rampage. That implies that if it only stood there, it is not. But then the ברייתא says that if it hid from them, it is not on a rampage. That implies that if it stood there, it is!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a contradiction inside the ברייתא about an animal that neither chases nor hides, but simply stands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא never mentions 'standing' directly. Each clause hints at the standing case through a דיוק (inference). The chasing clause implies that standing is not a rampage, while the hiding clause implies that standing is a rampage.

keyTerms.meaning: and then you said (introduces the clashing clause)

steps.confusionAlert: Neither clause says 'standing' outright. Both rulings on standing are inferences (the word הָא signals 'which implies'), and that is why they can clash.

phrases.english: If it saw two people
and ran after them, it is on a rampage;
which implies: if it stands, it is not on a rampage.
And then you said:
if it hid from them, it is not on a rampage;
which implies: if it stands, it is on a rampage!
phrases.notes: Second inference, which clashes with the first.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After settling the city/day contradiction in Step 23, the גמרא finds a second internal contradiction in the behavior tests from Step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two behavior clauses of the ברייתא (chasing versus hiding)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The two clauses lead to opposite implied rulings about a standing animal.

steps.title: It depends on whether a marsh is nearby
steps.stepSummary: The two clauses speak about different fields: one near a marsh and one far from a marsh.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not difficult. One case is a field near a marsh, and the other case is a field that is not near a marsh.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by placing each clause in a different location.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Near a marsh, an animal can stand calmly because it knows it can escape into the marsh at any moment, so standing is not a sign of a rampage. Far from any marsh, a normal animal would hide or flee, so standing boldly shows it has lost its fear, and that counts as משולחת.

keyTerms.meaning: marsh or swamp (a wild animal's refuge)

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
here, it is in a field near a marsh,
phrases.notes: Standing there is normal, so it is not a rampage.

phrases.english: there, it is in a field that is not near a marsh.
phrases.notes: Standing there is bold, so it is a rampage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each clause refers to a different location
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The clauses seemed to rule on the same standing animal in the same setting.
steps.terutzMaskana: Standing near a marsh is not a rampage. Standing far from a marsh is a rampage.

steps.title: Why doesn't eating both victims count, if even chasing does?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says killing two people and eating both is not a rampage, yet even chasing people is a rampage.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא says that if it tore apart two people at once and ate one of them, it is on a rampage. If it ate both of them, it is not. But didn't you say that even if it only chased people, it is on a rampage?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes another clause of the ברייתא and challenges it against the chasing rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating both victims shows the animal killed only for food, which is normal behavior. Still, killing two people is far more extreme than merely chasing them. So if chasing alone counts as משולחת, killing two people should surely count too.

keyTerms.meaning: but didn't you say (introduces a challenge)

phrases.english: If it tore apart two people at once
and ate one of them, it is on a rampage;
if it ate both of them, it is not on a rampage.
But didn't you say that even if it merely ran after them, it counts?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new internal challenge to the ברייתא's behavior tests.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that killing two people and eating both is not a rampage
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: This is a קל וחומר-style argument: if mild aggression (chasing) counts, then killing two people should certainly count.

steps.title: The eating case happens in the marsh
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that the 'ate both' case is about an animal in its own marsh territory.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: when that ruling is taught, it is about an animal in a marsh.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers that the 'ate both' ruling is about a different setting: the marsh, where the animal lives.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In its own home, it is natural for a wild animal to attack people who come in, so killing and eating there does not show rampaging behavior. The chasing rule, by contrast, is about animals in places where people live or work.

keyTerms.meaning: an אמורא who resolves this difficulty and the next one (the hunter's hut)

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
When that ruling was taught, it was about an animal in a marsh.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: כִּי תָּנֵי הָהִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting one ruling to a specific setting (the animal's own habitat)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Killing two people and eating both seemed to happen in an ordinary setting, which would make it more extreme than chasing.
steps.terutzMaskana: In the marsh, attacking and eating is natural, so it is not a rampage.

steps.title: Isn't snatching a baby from a roof obviously a rampage?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the ברייתא's baby case and asks why it even needs to be stated.
steps.simpleTranslation: Back to the ברייתא itself: if it climbed onto a roof and took a baby from a cradle, it is on a rampage. But that is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to quote the ברייתא and asks a פשיטא question: why would the ברייתא teach something so clear?
steps.deeperAnalysis: An animal climbing a house to snatch a baby is clearly abnormal and bold. The גמרא assumes every case in a ברייתא teaches something new, so a case this obvious seems to add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: back to the text itself (returning to the source quoted earlier)
it is obvious! (a challenge that the ruling teaches nothing new)

phrases.english: Returning to the text itself:
If it climbed onto the roof
and took a baby from a cradle, it is on a rampage.
That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the contradiction cycles and returns to a clause of the ברייתא from Step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's case of snatching a baby from a cradle
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The case seems too obvious to need teaching.

steps.title: The roof belongs to a hunter's hut
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that the case is about a hunter's hut out in the wild, so the ruling teaches something new.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: it is like the huts of hunters.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers that the roof in the ברייתא belongs to a hunter's hut in a wild area.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because a hunter's hut stands in the animals' own territory, one might think an attack there is natural. The ברייתא teaches that snatching a baby from a cradle still counts as משולחת even there.
steps.whatToRemember: A beast counts as משולחת only when its behavior is abnormal for its setting. Standing still depends on whether a marsh is nearby. Killing and eating in the marsh, its own home, is natural. Snatching a baby is a rampage even from a hunter's hut in the wild.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
It is like the huts of hunters.
phrases.notes: A shelter in a wild area, where an attack might seem natural.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge of Step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining the case so that the ruling teaches something new
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The case seemed to be about an ordinary house, which would make the ruling obvious.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even from a hunter's hut in the wild, snatching a baby is a rampage.

steps.title: Even a peaceful army passing through requires sounding the alarm
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's next case, 'for the sword,' and brings a ברייתא. It says the alarm is sounded not only for an enemy army, but even for a 'sword of peace,' an army just passing through.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said they sound the alarm 'for the sword.' The רבנן taught: The sword they mentioned does not only mean an army that comes to fight us. That is obvious. It means even a 'peaceful sword,' an army that is only passing through our land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It quotes the משנה's words 'for the sword' and brings a ברייתא that explains how far this rule goes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An army that comes to attack obviously calls for an alarm. The ברייתא adds something new: even an army with no plan to fight us, just marching through to another country, is also a reason to sound the alarm. The ברייתא uses the pattern 'it is not necessary to say X, but even Y' to show that the rule reaches further than we might expect.

keyTerms.meaning: 'For the sword': the words quoted from the משנה, one of the dangers that calls for sounding the alarm
A sword that is not peaceful: an enemy army coming to attack
A 'sword of peace': an army just passing through on its way elsewhere
'It is not necessary to say... rather even...': a pattern showing the rule goes further than the obvious case

steps.confusionAlert: A 'sword of peace' does not mean a friendly army or an ally. It means a foreign army that has no plan to attack us but is crossing our land to fight someone else.

phrases.english: [The משנה said: They sound the alarm] for the sword, etc.
phrases.notes: A quote from the משנה, opening a new topic

phrases.english: The Sages taught [in a ברייתא]:
The sword that they mentioned [in the משנה],
it is not necessary to say [that it includes]
a sword that is not of peace (an attacking army),
rather, even a sword of peace (an army just passing through).
phrases.notes: This is the new point of the ברייתא

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the wild-animal discussion (Steps 19-29) and begins the next case in the משנה, the sword.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The court sounds the alarm even for a 'sword of peace,' an army only passing through ארץ ישראל, not just for an attacking army.

steps.title: Proof from פרעה נכה and המלך יאשיהו
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא proves its point. There was never a more 'peaceful' army than that of פרעה נכה, yet המלך יאשיהו stumbled because of it. A verse is about to be quoted.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was no army more 'peaceful' than that of פרעה נכה, who was only passing through. Even so, המלך יאשיהו stumbled because of it, as the verse says:
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a historical proof that even a passing army is dangerous. It ends with 'as it says,' which sets up a verse quoted on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: פרעה נכה was only marching through ארץ ישראל to fight a different enemy. He had no plan to attack the Jews. Still, המלך יאשיהו went out against him and was killed, which shows that even a passing army can bring disaster. That is why the alarm is sounded even for a 'sword of peace.'

keyTerms.meaning: The Egyptian king who marched through ארץ ישראל to fight another empire
King Josiah, a righteous king of Judah who went out to fight פרעה נכה
Stumbled: here, came to harm (he was killed)
As it is said: introduces a verse

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the rule about passing armies comes from real history. Danger can come even when the other side has no plan to fight us.

phrases.english: For you have no sword of peace
greater than that of Pharaoh Neco,
phrases.notes: He was only passing through to fight elsewhere

phrases.english: and nevertheless
King Josiah stumbled through it,
as it is stated:
phrases.notes: The verse continues on the next amud

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁאֵין לְךָ חֶרֶב שֶׁל שָׁלוֹם יוֹתֵר מִפַּרְעֹה נְכֹה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the proof for the ruling in Step 30 that even a 'sword of peace' requires the alarm.
steps.raayaObject: That even a passing, non-hostile army is dangerous enough to require sounding the alarm.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The history of המלך יאשיהו, who was harmed by the passing army of פרעה נכה, supported by a verse (quoted next).
